content: Measles, mumps, rubella, and varicella are serious diseases that can result in severe complications, long-term disability, or even death. Despite the widespread use and established effectiveness of the trivalent MMR vaccine, public concerns about its safety have led to reduced vaccination rates in some countries. This review evaluates the effectiveness, safety, and potential adverse effects of the MMR vaccine, the MMR vaccine administered alongside the varicella vaccine (MMR+V), and the tetravalent MMRV vaccine in children up to 15 years of age. The review included 138 studies involving 23,480,668 participants. Of these, 51 studies (10,248,159 children) assessed vaccine effectiveness, while 87 studies (13,232,509 children) examined the association between the vaccines and various adverse effects. The review incorporated 74 new studies since its last update in 2012. Effectiveness: The MMR vaccine was 95% effective in preventing measles after one dose and 96% effective after two doses, based on moderate-certainty evidence. In preventing measles transmission to household contacts, the vaccine was 81% effective after one dose, 85% effective after two doses, and 96% effective after three doses, though the evidence for these findings was of low certainty. Post-exposure prophylaxis with at least one dose of the vaccine was 74% effective in preventing measles, based on low-certainty evidence. The MMR vaccine containing the Jeryl Lynn mumps strain was 72% effective in preventing mumps after one dose and 86% effective after two doses, with moderate-certainty evidence. It was 74% effective in preventing mumps transmission to household contacts. The vaccine's effectiveness against rubella, using the BRD2 strain (used only in China), was 89%, based on moderate-certainty evidence. The MMRV vaccine was 95% effective in preventing varicella of any severity after two doses in children aged 11 to 22 months, with high-certainty evidence from a 10-year follow-up study. Safety: There is evidence of an association between MMR vaccines containing the Urabe and Leningrad-Zagreb mumps strains and aseptic meningitis. However, no such association was found for MMR vaccines containing the Jeryl Lynn mumps strain. MMR, MMR+V, and MMRV vaccines containing the Jeryl Lynn strain are associated with an increased risk of febrile seizures. Febrile seizures occur in 2% to 4% of healthy children at least once before the age of 5. The estimated risk of vaccine-induced febrile seizures is 1 per 1,150 to 1 per 1,700 doses administered. There is evidence of an association between MMR vaccination and idiopathic thrombocytopaenic purpura (ITP). However, the risk of ITP after vaccination is lower than the risk following natural infection with these viruses. Natural infection results in approximately 5 cases of ITP per 100,000 individuals annually, while the risk after vaccination is estimated at 1 case per 40,000 doses. No evidence supports an association between MMR immunisation and encephalitis or encephalopathy, based on low-certainty evidence. Similarly, no association was found between MMR vaccination and autism spectrum disorders, based on moderate-certainty evidence. There is insufficient evidence to determine whether MMR vaccination is associated with inflammatory bowel disease. Additionally, no evidence supports an association between MMR immunisation and cognitive delay, type 1 diabetes, asthma, dermatitis/eczema, hay fever, leukemia, multiple sclerosis, gait disturbances, or bacterial/viral infections. Conclusions: The available evidence supports the safety and effectiveness of MMR, MMR+V, and MMRV vaccines, reinforcing their use in mass immunisation programs. Efforts to eradicate these diseases globally should consider the epidemiological and socioeconomic contexts of individual countries and aim to achieve high vaccination coverage. Further research is needed to determine whether the protective effects of these vaccines diminish over time.
